cards.q: What is the difference between a static library and a DLL?
cards.a:
A static library's code is copied into the `.exe` at link time; a DLL's code stays in its own file and is mapped into the process when it is loaded

Static code joins the executable when it is linked. A DLL stays a separate file, so it can be shared between processes and replaced on its own.
cards.lessonTitle: What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them

cards.q: Which of these is a real reason to put code in a DLL?
cards.a:
Several programs can share one copy, and that part can be updated without rebuilding them

DLLs give sharing, separate updates, plugins, hot reload and a C interface for other languages. They do not make calls faster: a call goes through an extra indirect jump.
cards.lessonTitle: What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them

cards.q: What file format do DLLs and executables share?
cards.a:
The PE (Portable Executable) format

Both `.dll` and `.exe` files are PE files with the same headers and sections; a DLL simply has no `main` and is not run on its own.
cards.lessonTitle: What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them

cards.q: What can a DLL not do on its own?
cards.a:
Run: it has no `main` of its own

A DLL holds code and data, and can import from other DLLs, but it only runs once a program has loaded it into its process.
cards.lessonTitle: What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them

cards.q: Two programs use the same DLL. What does Windows share between them?
cards.a:
The DLL's code pages in physical memory, until a process writes to a page

Code pages are read-only and shared. A page a process writes to, such as the DLL's global data, becomes that process's own copy.
cards.lessonTitle: What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them

cards.q: Which table lists the functions a DLL offers to other modules?
cards.a:
The export table

Imports are what a module needs from others; exports are what it offers. The relocation table lists addresses to fix if it loads at a different base.
cards.lessonTitle: What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them

cards.q: Which list gives the loader's steps for one module in the right order?
cards.a:
Find the file, map it, relocate if needed, load its dependencies, bind its imports, run its initialisation

A module's imports can only be bound once its dependencies are loaded, and its initialisation (DllMain) runs last, when everything it calls is ready.
cards.lessonTitle: How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process

cards.q: What is an RVA?
cards.a:
An offset from the module's base address in memory

A relative virtual address stays the same wherever the module lands: the real address is the base plus the RVA. The address a module asks for is its preferred base, not an RVA.
cards.lessonTitle: How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process

cards.q: Why are a DLL's dependencies initialised before the DLL itself?
cards.a:
So that when the DLL's initialisation runs, every DLL it calls into is already ready

The loader walks the dependency graph depth-first, dependencies first. It does not follow the order you list imports in.
cards.lessonTitle: How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process

cards.q: Two DLLs in a program both depend on math.dll. How many times is math.dll mapped?
cards.a:
Once; the second request increases its reference count

The loader keeps a list of modules already in the process and reuses them.
cards.lessonTitle: How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process

cards.q: A module's preferred base is 0x180000000 but it lands at 0x7FF600000000. A stored address was 0x180001234. What is it after relocation?
cards.a:
0x7FF600001234

The fix-up adds (actual base - preferred base) to every listed address, so the RVA 0x1234 is kept: 0x7FF600000000 + 0x1234. Adding the actual base to the whole old address would count the preferred base twice.
cards.lessonTitle: How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process

cards.q: Which step of loading produces "The procedure entry point could not be located"?
cards.a:
Binding imports against the DLL's export table

The DLL was found and mapped, but it does not export that name. A missing file gives the "was not found" message instead.
cards.lessonTitle: How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process

cards.q: What does `__declspec(dllexport)` do?
cards.a:
It puts the function, class or variable into the DLL's export table so other modules can find it

`dllexport` is the DLL side. Calling through the import table is what `dllimport` does on the program's side.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First DLL in Visual Studio

cards.q: Which two files from a DLL build do you need, and when?
cards.a:
The import `.lib` at link time and the `.dll` at run time

The import library tells the linker of each calling program which DLL each function is in; the DLL itself is loaded at run time, next to the program. The `.pdb` is debug symbols and the `.exp` can be ignored.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First DLL in Visual Studio

cards.q: What does the `STONEMATH_EXPORTS` symbol do?
cards.a:
It is defined only in the DLL project, so the shared header picks `dllexport` there and `dllimport` everywhere else

Only the DLL project defines it. Defining it in the program as well makes the program's header say `dllexport` and causes confusing link errors.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First DLL in Visual Studio

cards.q: Which file does the program's linker need?
cards.a:
StoneMath.lib, the import library

The import library tells the linker which DLL each function lives in. The DLL itself is needed when the program runs.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First DLL in Visual Studio

cards.q: Why does the header switch between dllexport and dllimport?
cards.a:
One header must export when building the DLL and import elsewhere

The same declaration is used by both sides: the project that defines STONEMATH_EXPORTS is the DLL and exports; every other user of the header imports.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First DLL in Visual Studio

cards.q: A helper function in stone_math.cpp has no STONEMATH_API. Can StoneDemo call it?
cards.a:
No; it is in the DLL's code but not in its export table

Only exported names can be found from outside the module. Calling it from StoneDemo gives LNK2019, an unresolved external symbol.
cards.lessonTitle: Your First DLL in Visual Studio

cards.q: What three things does an export table entry hold?
cards.a:
A name (optional), an ordinal, and the RVA of the function or variable

Each entry has an optional name, a number unique in the DLL, and where the export starts relative to the DLL's base.

cards.q: Which is a good reason to use a .def file?
cards.a:
It gives fixed ordinals and lets an export use another name

A `.def` file can export a function under a different name than the code uses, and it also exports plain names without changing the code. `__declspec(dllexport)` exports functions too, so a `.def` file is never required.

cards.q: Why prefer exporting a function such as `int stonesCreated()` over exporting a variable?
cards.a:
A function can change internally; a variable fixes its type for good

A function can change how it works without breaking callers, while an exported variable fixes its type and meaning for every program. Exported variables do work, and both modules see the same memory.

cards.q: What does NONAME mean in a .def file?
cards.a:
The function is exported by ordinal only, with no name

The export table holds no name for it, so other modules can only find it by its number.

cards.q: Why are ordinals risky across versions?
cards.a:
A reused ordinal makes old programs silently call the wrong function

Names describe what you call; numbers only describe a position, so if an ordinal later refers to a different function nothing warns you. Ordinals are actually faster to look up than names.

cards.q: Which .def line exports the function `stack_impl` under the public name `Stack`?
cards.a:
Stack = stack_impl

The public name comes first, then the internal one.

cards.q: What is the import address table?
cards.a:
An array of slots in a module, one per imported function, that the loader fills with the real addresses; calls into DLLs jump through them

The list of what a DLL offers is its export table. The IAT slots hold placeholders in the file, because the real addresses are only known at load time.

cards.q: Why does `__declspec(dllimport)` make calls slightly better?
cards.a:
The compiler calls through the IAT slot directly, with no stub

Without `dllimport` the call still works, through a small stub the linker adds that then jumps through the slot: one extra jump.

cards.q: Why should a published DLL never remove an export?
cards.a:
Programs that import that name will no longer start

Load-time linking resolves every import before `main`, and the loader refuses to start a program whose imported name is missing.

cards.q: What does an import library contain?
cards.a:
The DLL's export names and which DLL each is in, but no code

It lets the linker connect calls to the DLL without including its code. Debug symbols are in the `.pdb`.

cards.q: Who fills in the import address table?
cards.a:
The loader, when the program starts

The real addresses are not known until the DLL is mapped.

cards.q: A program imports stackWeight but the DLL on disk does not export it. What happens?
cards.a:
The program fails to start with "procedure entry point could not be located"

Load-time linking resolves every import before `main`, so the program never starts.

cards.q: How do you tell whether a DLL is 32-bit or 64-bit?
cards.a:
`dumpbin /headers` shows the machine type: x86 or x64

The headers hold the machine type. Names are no guide: 64-bit Windows keeps its 64-bit DLLs in a folder called System32.
cards.lessonTitle: Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies

cards.q: Where can you see which file a running program actually loaded for a DLL?
cards.a:
In the debugger's Modules window (the Path column), or in Process Monitor

`dumpbin /dependents` only lists DLL names the program needs, not which copy Windows picked at run time.
cards.lessonTitle: Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies

cards.q: What does the Dependencies tool add over dumpbin?
cards.a:
The whole dependency tree, with missing DLLs highlighted

dumpbin shows one module at a time; Dependencies follows every DLL's own dependencies recursively, handles API set names correctly and marks in red what it cannot find.
cards.lessonTitle: Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies

cards.q: Which command answers "which DLLs does this program need directly?"
cards.a:
dumpbin /dependents

/imports gives the same list plus every function; /dependents is the short version.
cards.lessonTitle: Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies

cards.q: How can you see every folder Windows tried while looking for a DLL?
cards.a:
Record the start in Process Monitor, filtered on .dll

Process Monitor records every path Windows tried, including the ones that failed with NAME NOT FOUND. dumpbin only lists which DLLs are imported, not where they were searched for.
cards.lessonTitle: Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies

cards.q: What does a name ending in D, such as MSVCP140D.dll, tell you?
cards.a:
It is the debug C++ runtime, used by Debug builds

The program was built in Debug. Debug runtimes are only installed with Visual Studio, so a Debug build will not run on most other machines.
cards.lessonTitle: Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies

cards.q: What is a decorated (mangled) name?
cards.a:
The compiler's symbol for a C++ function, encoding its scope and types

It encodes the scope, calling convention, return and parameter types so overloads can coexist, because the linker only compares strings. It is not compression or protection: `undname` turns it back into the declaration.

cards.q: What does `extern "C"` give up?
cards.a:
Overloading, and C++-only types in the signature if other languages are to call the function

Only the name and signature follow C rules. The body is still ordinary C++.

cards.q: What does `?reset@@YAXXZ` decode to?
cards.a:
`void __cdecl reset(void)`

`YA` is a free `__cdecl` function, the first `X` is the `void` return, and `XZ` means no parameters. An `int` would be `H`.

cards.q: Why does C++ decorate function names?
cards.a:
So overloads with the same name get different linker symbols

The linker only compares names, so the types have to be part of the name. Tools such as `undname` turn a decorated name straight back into the declaration.

cards.q: What is the MSVC decorated name of `int twice(int)`?
cards.a:
?twice@@YAHH@Z

`H` for the `int` return, `H` for the one `int` parameter, then `@Z`. `N` would be `double`, and `XZ` is a `void` function with no parameters.

cards.q: What does extern "C" change about a function?
cards.a:
Its linkage: a plain, undecorated name and no overloading

Only the name and signature follow C rules; the body is ordinary C++ compiled by the C++ compiler.

cards.q: What does a calling convention decide?
cards.a:
Where arguments and results go and who cleans up the stack

It also fixes which registers a function may change: the low-level agreement every call relies on. On 32-bit Windows it also changes the exported name, but that is a side effect, not its purpose.

cards.q: Why does the calling convention matter more across a DLL boundary than inside one program?
cards.a:
The two sides were compiled separately and may not agree

Inside one program the compiler uses one convention everywhere; across a DLL nothing guarantees agreement unless the interface says so. Nothing converts between conventions at the boundary.

cards.q: On 32-bit Windows, what are the exported names of `extern "C" int f(int, double)` as `__cdecl` and as `__stdcall`?
cards.a:
`_f` and `_f@12`

`__cdecl` adds a leading underscore; `__stdcall` also adds `@` and the bytes of arguments: 4 for the `int` plus 8 for the `double`.

cards.q: How many calling conventions does ordinary x64 Windows code use?
cards.a:
One: the Microsoft x64 convention

`__stdcall` and `__cdecl` still compile on x64, but they are ignored.

cards.q: What is the 32-bit exported name of extern "C" int __stdcall area(int, int)?
cards.a:
_area@8

`__stdcall` adds a leading underscore and `@` plus the bytes of arguments. `@area@8` is the `__fastcall` form.

cards.q: On 32-bit Windows, a __stdcall function is called as if it were __cdecl. What goes wrong?
cards.a:
The arguments are popped twice, corrupting the stack pointer

`__stdcall`'s callee and `__cdecl`'s caller both clean up, so the stack pointer is off by the size of the arguments. Both conventions return values the same way.

cards.q: What do LoadLibraryW, GetProcAddress and FreeLibrary each do?
cards.a:
Map a DLL and return its handle; look up an exported function's address by name; drop one reference and unmap the DLL when none remain

`GetProcAddress` only returns an untyped address, and `FreeLibrary` unmaps the DLL only when its reference count reaches zero.
cards.lessonTitle: Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress

cards.q: What happens to function pointers from a DLL after its last FreeLibrary?
cards.a:
They dangle: the code they point to is no longer mapped, so calling them crashes

Nothing resets your pointers. Drop them before the last `FreeLibrary`.
cards.lessonTitle: Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress

cards.q: Which of these does run-time loading make possible that load-time linking does not?
cards.a:
Starting without the DLL and choosing between several DLLs while running

Run-time loading also allows plugins found at run time and unloading and reloading code. `GetProcAddress` can still only find exported names.
cards.lessonTitle: Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress

cards.q: LoadLibraryW fails with error 126, but StoneMath.dll is next to the program. What is the most likely cause?
cards.a:
One of StoneMath.dll's own dependencies is missing

126 means "module not found", and it covers every module the loader needs. A wrong architecture gives 193 instead.
cards.lessonTitle: Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress

cards.q: A DLL is loaded twice and freed once. Is it still mapped?
cards.a:
Yes; its reference count is still 1

Each LoadLibrary is matched by one FreeLibrary.
cards.lessonTitle: Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress

cards.q: Why must the function pointer type match the DLL's function exactly?
cards.a:
The address is untyped, so a wrong cast breaks the call silently

`GetProcAddress` looks up a name only; the type exists only in your cast, so a mismatch passes arguments the wrong way with no compiler error.
cards.lessonTitle: Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress

cards.q: What is the loader lock?
cards.a:
A process-wide lock held while modules load, unload and run DllMain

Global constructors run under it too. Any other thread that wants to load or unload a module waits for it, which is why waiting inside DllMain is dangerous.

cards.q: Why can creating and waiting for a thread in DllMain deadlock?
cards.a:
The new thread needs the loader lock that the waiting DllMain holds

A new thread must send DLL_THREAD_ATTACH notifications, which need the loader lock. Creating the thread is allowed; waiting for it is the problem.

cards.q: What is the alternative to doing work in DllMain?
cards.a:
Init and shutdown functions the program calls, or lazy setup

The program calls init after loading and shutdown before unloading, or the DLL sets itself up on first use; neither runs under the loader lock. Global constructors run under the loader lock too.

cards.q: Which of these is safe inside DllMain?
cards.a:
Calling DisableThreadLibraryCalls

Anything that loads modules or waits for another thread can deadlock on the loader lock.

cards.q: When do the constructors of a DLL's global objects run?
cards.a:
At DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH, before your DllMain

The CRT's entry point constructs globals as part of attaching the DLL, under the loader lock, then calls your DllMain.

cards.q: What should a DLL that needs worker threads do instead of starting them in DllMain?
cards.a:
Offer an init function the program calls after LoadLibrary returns

Outside DllMain the loader lock is not held, so waiting and loading are safe.

cards.q: Why can freeing memory across a DLL boundary crash?
cards.a:
The modules may use separate C runtime heaps that don't share blocks

So one module frees a block the other's heap never allocated. Both modules live in the same address space; the problem is two heaps (a static CRT, or Debug versus Release).
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees

cards.q: Which set follows the rule "whoever allocates, frees"?
cards.a:
The library offers a free function; the caller provides the buffer; or objects come with a create/destroy pair

In each pattern the module that allocated a block is the one that frees it.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees

cards.q: Why not pass std::string across a DLL's C interface?
cards.a:
Its layout and allocator can differ between the two modules

So one side may misread or free the other's buffer. Inside a DLL use any C++ you like; at its C interface use pointers, sizes and plain structs.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees

cards.q: A DLL built with /MT allocates with new. The program frees with delete. What is wrong?
cards.a:
The DLL's static CRT has its own heap, separate from the program's

So the program frees memory its heap never allocated. Each statically linked CRT has its own heap.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees

cards.q: Which interface follows the "whoever allocates, frees" rule?
cards.a:
A create function paired with a destroy function in the same DLL

The DLL's destroy function frees with the same heap that allocated.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees

cards.q: In the "caller provides the buffer" pattern, why call the function first with a null buffer?
cards.a:
To find out how large a buffer is needed

The caller then allocates exactly enough and calls again.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees

cards.q: What does an exception barrier do?
cards.a:
It wraps an exported function's body in try/catch and returns an error code instead of letting any exception escape

It catches specific exceptions first, then `std::exception`, then `catch (...)`, and turns each into an error code.
cards.lessonTitle: Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary

cards.q: Which three things must match for C++ types to cross a DLL boundary safely?
cards.a:
Compiler and library version, build configuration and CRT setting

`std::string` and `std::vector` change layout between compiler versions and between Debug and Release (the iterator debug level), and the CRT setting must give one shared heap.
cards.lessonTitle: Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary

cards.q: How do you pass a list of numbers through a C interface?
cards.a:
As a pointer to the first element and a count

A pointer and a count are plain C types any language can pass; inside, the DLL can wrap them in a `std::span` for comfortable C++ again.
cards.lessonTitle: Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary

cards.q: Why must exceptions not leave an extern "C" function?
cards.a:
Other callers can't handle C++ exceptions, and they cross heaps

Callers written in other languages, or built differently, cannot catch C++ exceptions, and the exception object crosses heaps. Catch at the edge and return an error code; `try` blocks are fine inside an `extern "C"` function.
cards.lessonTitle: Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary

cards.q: In an exception barrier, why does catch (const std::exception&) come after catch (const std::invalid_argument&)?
cards.a:
Catch clauses are tried in order, so the general one would otherwise catch everything first

Specific types first, then the base class, then catch (...).
cards.lessonTitle: Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary

cards.q: When is exporting std::string from a DLL acceptable?
cards.a:
When both sides always build together with the same settings

That is an internal DLL built with the same compiler and settings as its users; a public one uses C types.
cards.lessonTitle: Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary

cards.q: What is an opaque handle?
cards.a:
A pointer to a type that is declared but not defined in the public header

Callers can store and pass the pointer but never see the type's size or members, so their code never depends on its contents.

cards.q: Why prefix every exported name, as in `xenon_world_create`?
cards.a:
All exported names share one namespace, so a prefix avoids clashes

Another library's `create` would clash with yours, and `<library>_<type>_<verb>` also lets callers guess names. Name decoration is turned off by `extern "C"`, not by a prefix.

cards.q: Which list contains only changes that are safe after version 1 is published?
cards.a:
Adding a function, adding a result code, changing what is behind an opaque handle

Removing or renaming functions, changing parameter types and changing a visible struct's layout all break programs already built against version 1.

cards.q: What is binary compatibility?
cards.a:
Programs already compiled against the old DLL keep working with the new one, without recompiling

That is the promise a DLL interface makes. Still compiling is source compatibility, which is weaker; the new DLL may also export more functions.

cards.q: Why can a library change everything behind an opaque handle?
cards.a:
Because callers only hold a pointer and never see the type's size or members

The callers' compiled code does not depend on the definition, so members can be added, reordered or replaced.

cards.q: Which change breaks binary compatibility?
cards.a:
Changing a parameter from `int32_t` to `int64_t`

Old programs still pass 4 bytes where the new DLL reads 8. The other changes leave existing programs' compiled calls valid.

cards.q: Which set of rules keeps result codes stable across versions?
cards.a:
Give every code an explicit number that never changes, add new codes only at the end, and treat unknown nonzero codes as failure

Programs built against version 1 have the numbers baked in, and later versions will return codes they have never seen.
cards.lessonTitle: Error Reporting Across a C API

cards.q: How does a library report a detailed error message through a C interface?
cards.a:
It stores a per-thread message that a function copies into a buffer

On failure it saves the message for the current thread, and a function copies it into a caller-provided buffer: the `GetLastError` pattern. Exceptions and `std::string` must not cross a C boundary, and a single global would be overwritten by other threads.
cards.lessonTitle: Error Reporting Across a C API

cards.q: When is returning a `const char*` across the boundary safe?
cards.a:
When it points to a string literal or other data that lives as long as the DLL and is never freed

A string literal sits in the DLL's read-only data. A `std::string`'s buffer dangles as soon as the string changes or is destroyed.
cards.lessonTitle: Error Reporting Across a C API

cards.q: Version 3 of a DLL returns code 6, which version 1's program does not know. What should the program do?
cards.a:
Treat it as a failure, because every nonzero code means failure

Unknown nonzero codes must count as failures; that is what lets the set of codes grow.
cards.lessonTitle: Error Reporting Across a C API

cards.q: Why is the last error message stored in a `thread_local` variable?
cards.a:
So threads calling the library at the same time cannot overwrite each other's message

Each thread reads the message of its own last failure. With one global, thread B could replace thread A's message before A reads it.
cards.lessonTitle: Error Reporting Across a C API

cards.q: Why do the functions return `int32_t` rather than the `xenon_result` enum type?
cards.a:
The size of a C enum is not guaranteed to be the same for every compiler

A fixed-size integer keeps the ABI exact. Returning an enum is legal C, but its size could differ between the DLL's and the caller's compiler.
cards.lessonTitle: Error Reporting Across a C API

cards.q: What are the rules for growing a versioned struct?
cards.a:
Add members only at the end, never remove, reorder or resize one, and give each new member a default

Old programs know the old offsets, so every existing member must stay where it is, and callers that did not send a new member need a sensible default.

cards.q: How does the library decide whether a member is present in the caller's struct?
cards.a:
It checks that the caller's `size` is at least the member's offset plus the member's size

`size >= offsetof(T, member) + sizeof(member)`. A nonzero value says nothing, and comparing with the whole newest struct would reject every older caller.

cards.q: Why are function tables popular for plugin and graphics APIs?
cards.a:
One exported function gives the whole interface, and the table itself can be versioned and grown

One `GetProcAddress` gets everything, and the table starts with `size` and `version` like any versioned struct.

cards.q: Why does a versioned struct start with its size?
cards.a:
So the library can tell which members the caller's version of the struct contains

Old callers send smaller sizes, and the library only reads what is there.

cards.q: A member `seed` sits at offset 16 and is 4 bytes. The caller's size is 16. Is `seed` present?
cards.a:
No, it would need a size of at least 20

Present means size >= offset + sizeof(member), so 16 + 4 = 20 bytes at least.

cards.q: What does a function table export instead of many separate functions?
cards.a:
One function returning a versioned struct of function pointers

The table can grow like any versioned struct, and the caller asks for the version it was built for.

cards.q: What are the three methods of `IUnknown`?
cards.a:
`QueryInterface` asks for another interface the object supports, `AddRef` adds a reference, `Release` drops one and deletes the object at zero

Every COM-style interface starts with these three. There is no virtual destructor: the object deletes itself in `Release`.

cards.q: How do COM-style interfaces gain new methods without breaking old callers?
cards.a:
A published interface never changes; new methods go in a new interface that callers request with `QueryInterface`

Even appending changes the published table that old code was compiled against; a new interface such as `IStone2` keeps the old one exactly as it was.

cards.q: Why does `Release` call `delete this` instead of the caller deleting the object?
cards.a:
So the memory is freed by the module that allocated it, whoever releases the last reference

Freeing in the DLL that called `new` avoids the mismatched-heap crash from lesson 2.05, and it only happens when the count reaches zero.

cards.q: Why can an abstract class with only pure virtual functions cross a DLL boundary between compilers on Windows?
cards.a:
Its layout, a vptr to a table in declaration order, is fixed by the ABI

The platform ABI fixes it as a single vptr to a table of function pointers in declaration order, the same layout as a C struct holding a pointer to a table of function pointers.

cards.q: Who deletes a reference-counted object?
cards.a:
The object itself, in `Release`, when the count reaches zero

`delete this` runs inside the module that allocated it, so no caller ever deletes it directly.

cards.q: A caller asks `QueryInterface` for an interface the object does not implement. What should it get?
cards.a:
A "not supported" result and a null pointer

The caller can then fall back to an older interface. Returning a different interface would let it call methods that are not there.

cards.q: What does each part of MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH mean for a DLL?
cards.a:
Major: a breaking change; minor: additions that keep compatibility; patch: fixes with no interface change

Only a major increase may break programs built against earlier versions; adding functions is a minor increase.

cards.q: What is the compatibility rule for a program built against version X.Y.Z?
cards.a:
It works with any DLL that has the same major X and a minor.patch of at least Y.Z

A newer minor only adds things; an older minor might lack a function the program needs; a different major may have changed anything.

cards.q: What was DLL Hell, and how does renaming the DLL for a new major version avoid it?
cards.a:
Installers replaced a shared DLL with an incompatible one of the same name; a new name lets both versions be installed side by side

Programs built for version 1 keep loading `xenon.dll` while version 2 programs load `xenon2.dll`, as the Visual C++ runtime does with `msvcp140.dll`.

cards.q: A DLL adds two new functions and changes nothing else. Its version was 1.6.3. What is the next version?
cards.a:
1.7.0

Additions without breaks are a minor increase, which resets the patch number to 0.

cards.q: A program was built against version 2.3.0. Which DLL version works with it?
cards.a:
2.5.1

It needs the same major and at least 2.3.0. 2.2.9 is too old and may lack a function; 3.0.0 may have broken anything.

cards.q: How do you ship a breaking version without breaking programs that use the old one?
cards.a:
Give the new major version a different DLL file name so both can be installed

Old programs keep loading the old file, so nothing they rely on changes.

cards.q: What does a header-only C++ wrapper add on top of a C interface?
cards.a:
RAII handles, exceptions and C++ types, compiled into the caller

It gives RAII ownership of handles, exceptions instead of result codes, and types such as `std::string`. Its code is compiled by the caller, so only the C functions cross the boundary.
cards.lessonTitle: Wrapping a C API in Modern C++

cards.q: What must the C destroy function accept for move-only wrappers to be simple?
cards.a:
A null handle, doing nothing, so a moved-from wrapper can be destroyed safely

After a move the source holds `nullptr`, and its destructor still calls `xenon_world_destroy`.
cards.lessonTitle: Wrapping a C API in Modern C++

cards.q: How does a reference-counting smart pointer such as `RefPtr` behave on copy and on destruction?
cards.a:
A copy calls `AddRef`; destruction calls `Release`

Each holder owns one reference, and the object deletes itself in `Release` when the count reaches zero.
cards.lessonTitle: Wrapping a C API in Modern C++

cards.q: Why is the C++ wrapper header-only?
cards.a:
It compiles into the caller, so only C crosses over

The wrapper's code is built into the caller's module with the caller's compiler and settings, so only C crosses the DLL boundary and its C++ types never meet another module's.
cards.lessonTitle: Wrapping a C API in Modern C++

cards.q: Why is the `World` wrapper move-only?
cards.a:
A copy would destroy the same handle twice

Ownership of a handle must belong to exactly one object; a move hands it over and leaves the source empty.
cards.lessonTitle: Wrapping a C API in Modern C++

cards.q: Is it safe for the wrapper's `check` function to throw an exception?
cards.a:
Yes; it is thrown and caught in the caller's module, never across the DLL boundary

The rule is about exceptions leaving the DLL, not about the caller's own code.
cards.lessonTitle: Wrapping a C API in Modern C++

cards.q: What is the standard search order for a desktop application (with safe DLL search mode)?
cards.a:
Application folder, System32, the 16-bit System folder, the Windows folder, the current directory, then PATH

The current directory was moved down to fifth place by safe DLL search mode, and PATH is always searched last.

cards.q: Which two checks come before any folder is searched?
cards.a:
Whether a module with that name is already loaded, and whether it is one of the known DLLs

A module already in the process is reused, and known DLLs such as `kernel32.dll` always come from `System32`.

cards.q: Why is relying on PATH for your own DLLs a bad idea?
cards.a:
It is searched last and differs per machine, so the wrong DLL can win

Something earlier on PATH with the same name wins, or none is found at all: the classic "works on my machine" story. Put your DLLs next to the `.exe` instead.

cards.q: Where does Windows look first for a DLL requested by name, after the already-loaded and known-DLL checks?
cards.a:
The folder of the application's `.exe`

That is why shipping DLLs next to the `.exe` is reliable.

cards.q: Why was the current directory moved later in the search order?
cards.a:
A file planted in the working directory could otherwise be loaded before the real system DLL

That change is safe DLL search mode. The working directory may be a downloaded folder or a network share that someone else controls.

cards.q: Can you replace `kernel32.dll` by putting your own copy next to your program?
cards.a:
No; it is a known DLL and always loaded from `System32`

Known DLLs bypass the folder search entirely.

cards.q: Which three things together make a program load only the DLLs it means?
cards.a:
Full paths from trusted folders, `SetDefaultDllDirectories`, and checked files

Full paths from a trusted folder stop guessing for run-time loads, `SetDefaultDllDirectories` at start-up restricts the search for name-only imports, and checking files before loading protects folders users can write to.
cards.lessonTitle: Loading Only the Files You Mean

cards.q: How do you get the folder of your own `.exe`?
cards.a:
Call `GetModuleFileNameW` with a null module handle, then take the parent folder

The current directory changes with shortcuts and file dialogs; `GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr, ...)` always gives the `.exe`'s own path.
cards.lessonTitle: Loading Only the Files You Mean

cards.q: How do you read a DLL's resources without running its code?
cards.a:
`LoadLibraryExW` with `LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_DATAFILE`

Usually together with `LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_IMAGE_RESOURCE`. Loaded as data, no `DllMain` runs and nothing is executable; a plain `LoadLibraryW` still runs its `DllMain`.
cards.lessonTitle: Loading Only the Files You Mean

cards.q: What does `SetDefaultDllDirectories(LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS)` remove from the search?
cards.a:
The current directory and the PATH folders

Only the application folder, `System32` and folders added with `AddDllDirectory` remain.
cards.lessonTitle: Loading Only the Files You Mean

cards.q: A plugin loaded by full path from `plugins\fog` needs `noise.dll` from the same folder. Which flag helps?
cards.a:
`LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR`

It adds the loaded DLL's own folder to the search for its dependencies; the application folder flag would look next to the `.exe` instead.
cards.lessonTitle: Loading Only the Files You Mean

cards.q: What is DLL planting?
cards.a:
Placing a file with a DLL's name where the search order finds it before the real one

Full paths and restricted search directories prevent it.
cards.lessonTitle: Loading Only the Files You Mean

cards.q: Which two linker settings turn on delay loading?
cards.a:
`/DELAYLOAD:name.dll` on the program, and linking `delayimp.lib`

Both go on the program; the DLL does not change, and you keep linking its import library as before.

cards.q: How does a program recover if a delay-loaded DLL is missing?
cards.a:
It checks with `__HrLoadAllImportsForDll` or sets a failure hook

`__HrLoadAllImportsForDll` tests availability first, and a failure hook (`__pfnDliFailureHook2`) can return a fallback. The failure is a structured exception, not a C++ exception, so a normal `catch` does not see it.

cards.q: Which two things cannot be delay-loaded?
cards.a:
Exported data used directly, and `kernel32.dll`

Only function calls go through thunks, and the delay-load helper itself needs `kernel32.dll`. Calls made under the loader lock should not be delay-loaded either.

cards.q: When is a delay-loaded DLL loaded?
cards.a:
The first time the program calls one of its functions

The thunk loads it on demand, so a program that never calls it never loads it.

cards.q: What changes in the DLL to make it delay-loadable?
cards.a:
Nothing; delay loading is set up on the program's linker

`/DELAYLOAD` and `delayimp.lib` go on the program that imports the DLL.

cards.q: Why is only the first call into a delay-loaded DLL slower?
cards.a:
The helper writes the real address into the import slot, so later calls skip the helper

After the first call, the slot holds the function's address and calls are as fast as normal imports.

cards.q: How is a four-part file version stored in `VS_FIXEDFILEINFO`?
cards.a:
As two 32-bit values (MS and LS) of two 16-bit parts

`dwFileVersionMS = major << 16 | minor` and `dwFileVersionLS = build << 16 | revision`, so installers can compare numbers.

cards.q: Which pairing of a way to provide the Visual C++ runtime with its drawback is correct?
cards.a:
App-local copies next to the `.exe`: you must update them yourself, because Windows Update does not

The redistributable needs an installer step but is updated by Windows Update; `/MT` needs no runtime DLLs but gives every module its own CRT and heap.

cards.q: Where should your own DLLs go when you ship?
cards.a:
Next to the `.exe`, with plugins in their own folders

The application folder is searched first, so your copies win without depending on PATH or the current directory. Plugins are loaded by full path.

cards.q: A file version is 2.4.1.0. What is `dwFileVersionMS`?
cards.a:
`2 << 16 | 4`

MS holds major (high 16 bits) and minor (low 16 bits); build and revision are in LS.

cards.q: Why should a shipped program never be a Debug build?
cards.a:
It needs debug runtime DLLs that normal machines don't have

The debug runtimes (`msvcp140d.dll`, `ucrtbased.dll`) are not redistributable and only exist where Visual Studio is installed.

cards.q: What is the usual way to make sure the Visual C++ runtime is on a user's machine?
cards.a:
Run the `vc_redist` installer from your installer

The redistributable is shared by all programs and kept up to date; copying only some DLLs fails on clean machines.

cards.q: Which list names only things that a DLL can do and a static library cannot?
cards.a:
Be updated without rebuilding programs, be loaded and unloaded while running, be called from other languages

A DLL also shares its code pages between processes. Cross-boundary optimisation and free use of templates belong to header-only libraries instead.

cards.q: When is a static library the right choice?
cards.a:
When nothing needs a DLL: it's simplest, with no extra files or ABI

A static library needs no extra files, no ABI design and no loading rules. Updating separately and calling from other languages are exactly the reasons to pick a DLL.

cards.q: How can one library be built either as a DLL or statically?
cards.a:
With an export macro that is empty when a STATIC symbol is defined

Otherwise the macro is `dllexport` when building the DLL and `dllimport` in programs; define `STONEMATH_STATIC` in both the library and the program for a static `.lib`. An import library contains no code, so renaming it does not make a static library.

cards.q: A library must be callable from C# and Python. What should it be?
cards.a:
A DLL with a C interface

Other languages can load DLLs and call C functions, but they cannot use C++ headers or `.lib` files.

cards.q: Which kind of package lets the compiler optimise across the boundary the most?
cards.a:
Header-only

The compiler sees all of the code in each program. A DLL allows no optimisation across the boundary, since calls go through the import table.

cards.q: Why do engines often use DLLs in development but static linking for shipping?
cards.a:
DLLs allow fast rebuilds and hot reload; static ships one simple file

Static linking gives one fast, simple executable to ship. The same source is built both ways with a switch in the export macro.

cards.q: What goes in a plugin contract header?
cards.a:
The contract's version, the host's function table, the plugin's function table, and the name and type of the one exported function

Both sides compile against it, and everything in it is plain C: function tables in both directions and one export with a fixed name.

cards.q: Which list gives the checks a host makes before keeping a plugin?
cards.a:
Loaded by full path, has the export, a valid table version, and `start` succeeds

It must be a `.dll` loaded by full path with safe search flags, and its table must be big enough with the right API version. Any failed step skips that plugin, unloads it again and carries on with the others.

cards.q: Why should a plugin do nothing in `DllMain`?
cards.a:
`DllMain` runs under the loader lock; real work belongs in `start`

`start` is called after loading completes. Lesson 2.04's rules apply: under the loader lock, loading other DLLs or waiting on threads can deadlock.

cards.q: Why does the plugin contract use tables of function pointers in both directions?
cards.a:
Neither side needs an import library for the other, and the tables can be versioned

One `GetProcAddress` gets the plugin's table, and the host passes its own table in `start`.

cards.q: A DLL in the plugin folder has no `xenon_get_plugin` export. What should the host do?
cards.a:
Log it, `FreeLibrary` it and carry on with the other files

Not every DLL in the folder is a plugin, and one bad file must not stop the others.

cards.q: What is the correct order for unloading a plugin?
cards.a:
Call `stop`, drop its pointers, then `FreeLibrary`

After `FreeLibrary`, none of the plugin's code or data exists any more, so `stop` and every pointer it gave you must be finished with first.

cards.q: What does the host do with a plugin's registrations when the plugin unloads?
cards.a:
Removes every registration with that plugin as owner, before calling `FreeLibrary`

The registrations hold function pointers into the plugin's code, which must be gone from the registry before the DLL is unmapped.

cards.q: Why should the registry copy the id string?
cards.a:
The plugin's string is in DLL memory and vanishes when it unloads

A `const char*` into an unloaded DLL dangles, and a copy can also be used safely as a map key. The plugin's string literal lasts exactly as long as the DLL.

cards.q: What are capabilities in a plugin contract?
cards.a:
Named, versioned features a plugin can require exactly as it uses them

For example `"stone_types": 2`, `"commands": 1`: the host starts a plugin only if each need is met with at least that version, so the contract can grow feature by feature. Dependencies on other plugins are a separate list.

cards.q: Why does the plugin pass an owner pointer when it registers something?
cards.a:
So the host can remove everything that plugin registered before unloading it

Removal by owner keeps the registry free of dangling pointers.

cards.q: Two plugins register the same id. What should the registry do?
cards.a:
Refuse the second registration and report the clash

Refusing makes the result independent of the order in which the directory listing returned the DLLs.

cards.q: In what order should plugins with dependencies be started?
cards.a:
Dependencies first, depth first, each started once

Like the Windows loader: a plugin's requirements must be running before it starts, and a missing requirement or a cycle means it is not started.

cards.q: Which describes the hot-reload loop correctly?
cards.a:
On a new complete build, load a fresh copy, swap to its table, then free the old copy

When the DLL's write time changes and the file is complete, copy it to a fresh name and load the copy. Loading a copy keeps the original writable, and the old copy is only freed after the new table is in place, so the game never runs without code.

cards.q: Why does each build's PDB need a unique name?
cards.a:
The debugger locks the PDB of the loaded DLL, so the linker could not overwrite it

The next link would fail to write `gameplay.pdb`. A unique name per build avoids the clash.

cards.q: Which list contains only things that become invalid after unloading the old DLL?
cards.a:
Its function pointers, its string literals, and vtables of objects it created

Static variables inside the DLL are also reset. Memory the host owns survives, which is why state lives there.

cards.q: Why does the host load a copy of the DLL instead of the DLL itself?
cards.a:
The loaded file is locked, so the next build couldn't write it

Windows locks a loaded DLL's file, and the original must stay writable for the compiler's next build.

cards.q: The host sees a new time stamp on `gameplay.dll`. Why might reloading straight away fail?
cards.a:
The linker may still be writing the file

Wait until the time stamp has been stable for a few checks, or until a lock file disappears.

cards.q: Which of these survives a hot reload?
cards.a:
Game state stored in memory the host owns

Everything inside the old DLL's image is gone after `FreeLibrary`; the host's memory is untouched.

cards.q: Which describes the host-owned-memory strategy?
cards.a:
The host allocates one memory block and passes it to the DLL every frame; the DLL keeps all state as plain data in it

Swapping the DLL leaves the block untouched, so the new code finds the state exactly as the old code left it.

cards.q: What makes state safe to keep across a reload?
cards.a:
Plain data with no pointers into the DLL, in memory the host owns

No vptrs, no pointers to the DLL's functions or string literals, and memory from the host rather than the DLL's heap. Anything that points into the old DLL's image dangles after `FreeLibrary`, and the DLL's statics reset on every reload.

cards.q: How do you handle a change in the state's layout?
cards.a:
Store a version number and migrate older versions to the new layout

Migration gives new fields defaults, and versions you cannot read start fresh. Reading old bytes with a new layout puts values in the wrong fields; it is lesson 3.03's versioned-struct problem again.

cards.q: Why must game state kept in host memory have no virtual functions?
cards.a:
Each object's vptr would point into the old, unloaded DLL

Plain data survives the swap; code pointers, including vtables, do not.

cards.q: The state gained a new field and the new DLL finds version 1 data. What should it do?
cards.a:
Migrate it: read the old layout, default the new field

Then write the new layout. A version number turns layout changes into a decision instead of garbage.

cards.q: Which strategy also works as a save-game system?
cards.a:
Save and restore through `save_state` and `load_state`

The DLL serialises its state to bytes, which can just as well be written to a file.

cards.q: Which course lessons does hot reload depend on?
cards.a:
Run-time loading (2.03), versioned tables (3.03), the reload loop (5.03) and host-owned, versioned state (5.04)

Hot reload loads the gameplay DLL with `LoadLibraryW`, reads its versioned table, swaps it in the reload loop, and keeps state in host memory.

cards.q: What makes plugin shutdown safe?
cards.a:
Stop each plugin in reverse order, unregister it, then `FreeLibrary`

Each plugin's `stop` runs in reverse load order and its registrations and pointers are dropped before it is unloaded. Anything left in a registry after `FreeLibrary` points into unmapped memory, and reverse order stops a plugin before the plugins it relies on.

cards.q: Why build the game with the gameplay code statically linked first?
cards.a:
To get the simplest version working before the DLL rules

Then the move to a DLL shows exactly what the boundary changes: globals, ownership and the interface.

cards.q: What should happen when a plugin's dependency is missing?
cards.a:
Skip that plugin with a clear message and keep running

One missing mod must not stop the game, and loading it anyway would only move the failure somewhere harder to read.

cards.q: The checklist says building while the game runs must never fail with a locked file. What makes that true?
cards.a:
Loading a copy of the gameplay DLL and giving each build's PDB a unique name

A loaded DLL and the PDB the debugger has open are both locked, so the host loads a copy and each link writes a new PDB (lesson 5.03).
